projects.title: Mutants of Agyr
projects.tagline: A post-apocalyptic zombie FPS — shoot your way through the ruins of Agyr to find the serum that can save the world.
projects.description:
Mutants of Agyr is a post-apocalyptic FPS built in Unity by a nine-person team — four developers and five artists. You are the last survivor, fighting through zombie-infested levels and completing quests to track down the serum that can rid the world of the mutants.

I owned the moment-to-moment gunplay and the progression systems: procedural gun feel (weapon sway, spring-driven recoil, camera shake, tracers), aim-down-sights, an ammo and reload loop tied into the grid inventory, and a ScriptableObject-based quest system with HUD. Because the whole team worked in the same scenes daily, I also built a suite of one-click editor tools so any teammate could wire my systems into a scene in seconds.

mechanics.subtitle: Spring-Driven Gun Feel
mechanics.description: Every shot raises a single onShotFired event that fans out to all the feedback at once: a recoil impulse on the arms rig, trauma-based camera shake, a camera pitch kick, muzzle flash VFX, and a pooled bullet tracer. The recoil itself is not an animation — it's a damped spring. The impulse is scaled by the spring's natural frequency so the designer-tuned kick values are the actual peak offsets, independent of spring stiffness, and the slightly underdamped settle bounce is what makes the gun read as heavy.

mechanics.subtitle: Auto-Aligning Aim Down Sights
mechanics.description: Hold right mouse to aim: the FOV blends from 90 to 65, weapon sway dampens, and movement slows — all driven by one 0-to-1 aim blend. The key trick is the scope point: the designer drops an empty GameObject on the gun's iron sight, and at startup the system computes the exact camera-space offset that brings that point to screen center. Adding ADS to a new weapon takes one empty transform — no per-gun offset tuning.

mechanics.subtitle: Inventory-Backed Ammo & Reload
mechanics.description: The gun's reserve ammo doesn't live on the gun — when a scene has the grid inventory, reserve ammo IS the ammo items in your backpack (one item = one full magazine), and reloading physically consumes an item. Scenes without an inventory fall back to a plain counter, so the same gun code runs everywhere. Every change fires a UnityEvent that keeps the ammo HUD in sync, and the reload triggers the arms and gun animators on the same frame so the two halves of the animation can never drift apart.

mechanics.subtitle: ScriptableObject Quest System
mechanics.description: Quests are ScriptableObject assets a designer can create straight from the Project window: a name, main-or-side flag, a list of objectives (kill enemies, collect items, or interact with world objects), guaranteed rewards, and a weighted random loot pool. The assets stay read-only at runtime — all progress counters live in the scene's quest manager, so quests reset cleanly with the scene and nothing ever mutates on disk. Enemies, pickups and interactables just report events; the manager routes them to whichever active quests care.

mechanics.subtitle: One-Click Editor Tooling
mechanics.description: Nine people shared the same scenes, so 'follow this 12-step setup document' was never going to survive the week. Instead every system I built ships with an editor tool under Tools > Senna — Setup Quests Scene, Setup Aim System, Wire Death Screen, and a dozen more. Each one is idempotent (every step checks what already exists before creating anything), wires private [SerializeField] references through SerializedObject exactly like the inspector would, creates missing ScriptableObject assets on the spot, and registers Undo for everything. A teammate can rebuild a broken scene's wiring in seconds.

projects.title: Replay Platformer
projects.tagline: A 3D platformer with tight movement mechanics and accessibility options.
projects.description:
A 3D platformer featuring tight movement mechanics and accessibility options. Playable with both controller and keyboard, including a web version for easy access.

I thoroughly enjoyed developing this game, focusing heavily on game feel and visual polish to ensure the movement felt satisfying and responsive. Implementing the wall jump mechanics presented an interesting challenge, but it was rewarding to perfect.

This project sparked my passion for creating advanced movement systems, and I look forward to exploring more complex mechanics in future projects.

mechanics.subtitle: Wall Jump - Detection
mechanics.description: Continuous raycasting detects nearby walls, allowing the player to enter a 'Wall Slide' state. This state reduces terminal velocity and enables the wall jump mechanic.

mechanics.subtitle: Wall Jump - Execution
mechanics.description: Executing a jump while sliding applies an instantaneous impulse force away from the wall and upwards. A brief 'jump lock' prevents immediate redirection, ensuring a consistent arc.

mechanics.subtitle: Enemy State Machine
mechanics.description: A robust Finite State Machine (FSM) manages complex enemy behaviors, including Roaming, Chasing, and Attacking. This architecture allows for clean transitions and modular AI logic.

mechanics.subtitle: Heatmap-Based Roaming
mechanics.description: To create more natural exploration, enemies use a 'visit count' heatmap. They periodically sample nearby points and prioritize those they haven't visited recently, ensuring thorough coverage of the environment.

projects.title: AI Agent Enemies
projects.tagline: A wave-based arena game featuring LLM-driven enemy AI.
projects.description: A prototype wave game built in Godot, starring an enemy AI powered by the Groq API (LLM). The AI acts as an unhinged villain, evaluating its health, the distance to the player, and whether it's stuck. It uses this context to choose from an arsenal of tactical behaviors (Chase, Attack, Search, Retreat, Strafe, Seek Cover) and dynamically reacts to the player's movements. This was an exploration into creating non-deterministic, highly responsive enemies in a traditional action-combat loop.

mechanics.subtitle: AI Decision Engine
mechanics.description: Enemies send their current state (health, memory of past events, distance, line of sight, etc.) to an LLM via the Groq API. The LLM evaluates the situation and decides on a tactical state, outputting both a strategic choice (like RETREAT or STRAFE) and an in-character thought bubble.
mechanics.code:
var prompt = """
You are the persistent, unhinged brain of an enemy in a 3D action game.
You remember everything that has happened this session...

=== CURRENT SITUATION ===
- Health: %s%%
- Distance to player: %s units
- Current state: %s
- Stuck on obstacle: %s

=== DECISION RULES ===
- If you have been stuck multiple times, try SEEK_COVER or STRAFE instead.
- If health < 30%%: strongly consider RETREAT.
- Do NOT keep repeating the same failing state.
"""

var body = JSON.stringify({
    "model": "groq/compound",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
})

mechanics.subtitle: Enemy State Machine
mechanics.description: The enemy's physical actions are executed via a robust Finite State Machine in GDScript. Once the LLM returns a decision like 'SEARCH', the enemy uses NavigationAgent3D to generate fan-out waypoints and investigates the last known player position, handling physics natively.

mechanics.subtitle: Movement & Momentum (Player)
mechanics.description: A responsive 3D character controller built entirely in GDScript, featuring jump buffering, coyote time, and heavy camera-shake juice upon taking hits or performing attacks.

mechanics.subtitle: Wave Spawning System
mechanics.description: A structured arena wave manager. Spawners operate independently, tracking active enemies and escalating wave counts, while dynamically spawning health pickups and monitoring for a total clear condition.

projects.title: VR Shooter
projects.tagline: A wave-based VR combat experience with modular AI enemies and satisfying feedback systems.
projects.description:
A VR shooter built in Unity featuring multiple enemy archetypes, a multi-phase boss, and a responsive combat feedback system. Each enemy type is built on a shared FSM base class, allowing for clean code reuse while enabling distinct behaviors — from exploding kamikazes to projectile-firing bartenders.

The project pushed me to think carefully about how enemy variety creates tactical depth without complexity, and how small feedback details like a damage vignette make hits feel impactful in VR.

mechanics.subtitle: FSM Enemy AI
mechanics.description: All enemies share a base Finite State Machine with four states: Roam, Lock, Attack, and Die. Roaming uses NavMesh sampling to pick valid positions in world geometry. State transitions use distance hysteresis — detecting the player at 20m but only losing sight at 24m — to prevent constant flickering between states.

mechanics.subtitle: Exploding Enemy (FSM Subclass)
mechanics.description: The ExplodingEnemy inherits from the base FSM and overrides the Attack state. Instead of melee damage it closes the gap and detonates — spawning a VFX prefab, dealing AOE damage, and destroying itself. This forces the player to kite and creates a different threat compared to melee enemies.

mechanics.subtitle: Bartender Enemy — Arcing Projectiles
mechanics.description: A stationary turret enemy that locks its rotation on the horizontal axis only (preventing jittery vertical aiming) then fires with a +1.5 unit upward bias. This creates naturally arcing bottle trajectories that feel dynamic without implementing real ballistic physics.

mechanics.subtitle: Boss — Multi-Cannon Fire Pattern
mechanics.description: The boss cycles through an array of fire points in round-robin order, creating spread bullet patterns. Each cannon fires a physics-driven projectile toward the player's current position. On defeat, a victory state triggers confetti and explosion effects.

mechanics.subtitle: Blood Vignette Damage Feedback
mechanics.description: Health is exposed as a C# property. Every time damage is taken, the delta is mapped to a screen-edge vignette alpha that fades over time. Larger hits produce a stronger flash. This runs entirely through the property setter — no polling, no Update check — keeping the feedback tightly coupled to the damage event.

projects.title: AI Data Entry Agent
projects.tagline: Turns invoices, timesheets and count sheets into clean Excel — live in production.
projects.description:
A document processing system that automates the most hated office job: manually retyping documents into Excel. Users upload invoices, payment emails, timesheets or warehouse count sheets — the system classifies each document, extracts every record in it through Groq's LLM API with a type-specific Pydantic schema, validates the results against business rules, and returns grouped tables with a multi-sheet Excel export.

Built with a pluggable registry pattern so adding a document type is one new schema class. Includes multi-user authentication, per-user data isolation, subscription-tier rate limiting, validation that flags suspect records for human review, and LLM-reported confidence scores. Deployed and live on Streamlit Cloud — benchmarked at 11/11 records extracted correctly across realistic test documents, including a deliberately messy payment email with two payments buried in chat text.

mechanics.subtitle: Pluggable Document Router
mechanics.description: Instead of hardcoding extraction logic per document type, the system uses a registry pattern. A zero-temperature LLM classifies the uploaded document (invoice, timesheet, inventory), then the router fetches the matching Pydantic schema from the registry and binds it to the LLM at runtime. Adding a new document type is one new schema class — no changes to the core pipeline. Unknown classifications fall back to the generic ledger schema instead of failing the file.
mechanics.code:
doc_type = router.classify(text)
plugin = registry.get(doc_type)

structured_llm = llm.with_structured_output(
    plugin.schema
)
result = structured_llm.invoke(prompt).model_dump()

mechanics.subtitle: Multi-Record Extraction with Review Flagging
mechanics.description: Real business documents rarely contain one record — a count sheet lists dozens of items, a payment email can mention several invoices, a timesheet covers multiple employees. Every document schema wraps a list of records; the pipeline explodes them into individual rows, and each row passes through a business-rule validator (date sanity, ISO currency codes, amount limits, VAT format). Rows that fail validation are flagged REVIEW so a human checks exactly the right ones — the difference between a demo and a tool a bookkeeper can trust.

mechanics.subtitle: Locale-Aware Number Parsing
mechanics.description: Real-world documents use inconsistent number formats — European invoices write 1.234,56 where US invoices write 1,234.56. The parser detects which separator is the thousands marker vs the decimal marker using position heuristics, then normalises to a canonical float. Currency symbols are also mapped to ISO codes, with unknown codes preserved rather than dropped.

mechanics.subtitle: Per-User Data Isolation
mechanics.description: Streamlit reruns the entire script on every interaction, which can cause data leakage between users in multi-tenant deployments. Each user gets their own isolated history file generated dynamically from their username. No user can ever see another user's processed documents, even across hot reloads.

mechanics.subtitle: Sliding-Window Rate Limiter
mechanics.description: A custom rate limiter that survives process restarts by persisting request timestamps to disk. It uses a sliding window (not fixed buckets) so limits are fair regardless of when in a window a user starts. Rate limits are subscription-tier-aware, and integrated cost tracking (tokens × pricing model) enforces per-user budgets automatically.
mechanics.code:
now = time.time()
window_start = now - self.window_seconds

self._requests[user] = [
    t for t in self._requests[user]
    if t > window_start
]

if len(self._requests[user]) >= self.max_requests:
    raise RateLimitExceeded()

self._requests[user].append(now)
self._persist()
